title: Police Cane Thousands of Cockroach Movement Supporters as 'Chalo Sansad' March Brings Delhi to a Standstill
excerpt: Around 10,000 protesters gathered at Jantar Mantar despite a police ban, demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over the NEET paper leak scandal.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Police clashed with 10,000 protesters at Jantar Mantar demanding Education Minister's resignation.
  • Hunger-striking activist Sonam Wangchuk's hospitalization intensified the protests against the NEET scandal.
  • CJP movement emerged after NEET paper leaks affected over two million students in May 2026.
  • Youth unemployment at 9.9% fuels frustrations among young Indians, driving protest participation.
  • Opposition parties increasingly support the movement, highlighting systemic corruption in education.

![Jantar Mantar. Key Takeaways Police clashed with 10,000 protesters at Jantar Mantar demanding Education Minister's resignation.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3f/Jantar_Mantar_at_Jaipur.jpg) > **""He has assured us that he will meanwhile speak internally."**
  • Police used lathi charges against thousands of Cockroach Janta Party supporters attempting to march on Parliament on the opening day of the monsoon session
  • Around 10,000 protesters gathered at Jantar Mantar despite police denying permission, demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation
  • Hunger-striking activist Sonam Wangchuk, forcibly hospitalized on Saturday, issued conditions from his hospital bed for ending his fast
  • CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was reportedly picked up by police as two other leaders held talks with Health Minister J.P. Nadda

Supporters of India's youth-led Cockroach movement clashed with police in New Delhi on Monday as they attempted to march on Parliament, escalating what has become the biggest public challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's third term.

Delhi Police deployed lathi charges and heavy barricades against the crowd of approximately 10,000 protesters who had gathered at Jantar Mantar — the designated protest site in the heart of the capital — despite authorities refusing permission for the march, according to Reuters.

Wangchuk's Impact on Protests
›Sonam Wangchuk's hospitalization galvanized protests.
›Protesters demand accountability for education failures.
›Wangchuk outlined conditions for ending his hunger strike.
›CJP leaders met with Health Minister J.P. Nadda.
![Sonam Wangchuk. Hunger-striking activist Sonam Wangchuk's hospitalization intensified the protests against the NEET scandal.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f2/Sonam_Wangchuk%2C_2017_%28cropped%29.jpg) https://x.com/Reuters/status/2079095255781999020

Television visuals showed officers caning protesters in heavily barricaded areas, though Delhi Police denied any use of force, stating the "protest is being handled professionally."

"The protest site has already run out of space and this can lead to an untoward situation."

— Sachin Sharma, Delhi's Deputy Commissioner of Police

Movement Galvanised After Wangchuk's Forced Hospitalisation

The confrontation intensified after police forcibly moved hunger-striking activist Sonam Wangchuk to hospital on Saturday, galvanising the movement. Thousands of supporters arrived through the night at Jantar Mantar for the march, timed to coincide with the opening day of Parliament's monsoon session.

In a handwritten note posted from his hospital bed on X, Wangchuk outlined three conditions for ending his fast: the government taking responsibility for recent education system failures and paper leaks, CJP protesters being allowed to reach Parliament with lawmaker assurances, or leaders of various parties meeting him in hospital with the same commitments.

Meanwhile, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was reportedly "picked up" by police even as two other movement leaders held a brief 10-minute meeting with Health Minister J.P. Nadda. "He has assured us that he will meanwhile speak internally. We are in that process," chief spokesperson Saurav Das said on X after the meeting.

Roots in NEET Paper Leak Scandal

The Cockroach Janta Party emerged after the national medical entrance exam (NEET) papers were leaked in May 2026, forcing more than two million students to retake the test. The movement initially gained traction online — amassing 22 million Instagram followers within days — before spilling onto the streets.

"All these leaders in power are illiterate and I am here to protest because we do not want question papers to leak," said Adi Nathan, a 21-year-old student from Meerut who had traveled roughly 100 kilometres to join the march. "This should come to an end."

The AAP party joined the protests on Monday, with senior leaders Manish Sisodia, Sanjay Singh, and Atishi gathering at Jantar Mantar. Sisodia cited at least 17 student suicides linked to the NEET scandal.

Youth Unemployment Fuels the Fire

The rise of the CJP reflects deeper frustrations among young Indians over high youth unemployment and frequent examination paper leaks. Government data shows unemployment at 9.9 percent for Indians aged 15 to 29, rising to 13.6 percent in urban areas — more than triple the overall rate of 3.1 percent.

Five Delhi Metro stations were shut over security concerns as authorities scrambled to contain the protests. Reports indicated internet services were also cut in parts of central Delhi.

The protesters chanted "Quit, quit" and "Dharmendra Pradhan quit, Narendra Modi quit" in Hindi as they arrived peacefully in rainy weather before the crackdown began. Opposition parties have increasingly backed the movement, with multiple leaders describing it as a legitimate expression of youth anger over systemic corruption in India's examination system.

![Delhi Metro. Five Delhi Metro stations were shut over security concerns as authorities scrambled to contain the protests.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/DelhiMetroYellowLine.JPG/3840px-DelhiMetroYellowLine.JPG)

nri_angle: India's largest youth-led protest in years highlights systemic failures in education that affect millions of families, including those with children in the diaspora considering Indian competitive exams.
